descriptions.description:
Research Purposes : How to Review this Package / Article ? 

Download the complete ZIP package ( Complete Technical Disclosure ) → UNZIP→ upload all extracted files into a dedicated AI Project/Workspace (not an ordinary chat) → Give Instruction to an AI to Read  00_READ_FIRST_AI_INSTRUCTIONS.md → use 01_AI_ANALYSIS_PROMPT.txt as a guide → independently verify findings against original WIPO sources.

Readers are strongly encouraged to use their own prompts for independent analysis rather than relying solely on the supplied prompt.

 

A Question for Readers

The relevant DAS disclosures were published from June 2026 by the World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO), Geneva. Meta publicly disclosed Muse/Sentinel on 8 September 2026.

Readers are requested to independently identify which technical elements were already disclosed in the earlier DAS materials and which elements are genuinely Meta-specific engineering choices.

The question is not whether Meta Muse/Sentinel reproduces every mechanism disclosed in DAS. The question is whether both architectures implement substantially the same underlying security principle and functional separation: an AI agent may propose an operation, but authority to make that operation effective resides outside the agent-controlled computation environment, at an independently enforced boundary.

Differences in containers, credential brokers, proxy implementations, policy engines, taint tracking, or hardware placement may represent alternative engineering choices within that broader architectural pattern.

 

An Open Challenge to GitHub Users: Independently Test, Compare, and Try to Break the DAS Execution-Finality Architecture

I am inviting developers, security researchers, protocol engineers, infrastructure architects, and technically curious GitHub users to independently examine the DAS execution-finality architecture.

The central principle is simple:

Computation is not authority to act.

A system may authenticate a user, execute code, generate an instruction, prepare a transaction, or construct a network request—but that does not necessarily mean the resulting action should automatically be allowed to become externally effective.

DAS explores a separate execution-finality layer in which a proposed action can remain non-effective until an independent enforcement mechanism determines whether that specific act is authorized to cross into the real world.

The Challenge

Do not accept my interpretation.

Download the technical materials, inspect the earlier disclosures, and try to answer independently:

Can the architecture be bypassed, reduced to conventional access control, or reproduced entirely from earlier known systems without relying on hindsight?

Researchers are specifically invited to look for:



alternative execution paths that bypass the finality boundary;

crash, timeout, rollback, replay, or race-condition failures;

capability reuse or substitution;

descriptor or canonicalization ambiguity;

alternate network, IPC, file, payment, GPU, storage, or actuation paths;

enforcement failures caused by legacy components;

contradictions between the claimed architecture and the disclosed embodiments;

prior art that performs the same complete sequence before the relevant priority dates.


A successful technical criticism is as useful as a successful validation.

DAS Mothership ↔ Meta Muse/Sentinel

Functional Terminology Mapping FAQ for Independent AI Review

Primary DAS source: PCT/IB2026/055615 — THE DAS PROTOCOLS, including Embodiment 84, Embodiment 85.B2, and the foundational definitions.

Meta comparison source: Meta's 8 September 2026 technical disclosure, How We Built Safety Into Muse.

Objective: Determine which architectural functions were expressly disclosed in DAS before Meta's public announcement, which are functionally analogous, which are implementation-specific, and which cannot be established as equivalent.

Important: Do not assume that similar terminology proves identical implementation, or that different terminology proves different technical function.




FAQ 1 — Is an Execution Handle (EH) functionally comparable to Meta's surrogate credential?

DAS source terminology:





Execution Handle (EH)




Externally presentable execution reference




Internally resolvable reference




Non-authoritative pointer, trigger, or handle




Protected live lookup




EH–EASO binding



Explicit DAS function: An EH identifies or references a governed execution context and enables protected authority state to be located, reconstructed, unsealed, or validated. It is not independently sufficient authority.

Meta function: hatch-authd mints surrogate credentials accessible to the agent runtime. Real credentials are retained outside the runtime cell.

AI comparison question: Do both architectures separate a runtime-visible reference from the protected authority required to perform an external action?

Qualification: EH is an execution reference, whereas Meta's surrogate is a credential placeholder. Compare their authority-indirection function without treating them as identical objects.

FAQ 2 — Is an EASO functionally comparable to Sentinel's protected permission state?

DAS source terminology:





Execution Authorization Scope Object (EASO)




Execution Authority Scope Object




Protected authority envelope




Purpose-bound authority




Destination-bound authority




Protected mutable state




EH–EASO inseparability



Explicit DAS function: EASO defines the authorized purposes, operations, destinations, time windows, jurisdictions, quotas, and other constraints associated with an EH or Candidate Act.

Meta function: Sentinel evaluates requests against permissions, credentials, destinations, and security policy.

AI comparison question: Do both systems retain permission authority outside the agent's direct control and evaluate concrete requested operations against that authority?

Qualification: Meta's documented policy and permission state should not automatically be treated as a single EASO-equivalent cryptographic object.

FAQ 3 — Is DAS Non-Bearer Authority comparable to Meta's surrogate-token restrictions?

DAS source terminology:





Non-Bearer Authority




Inert execution handle




Protected authority lookup




Credential-independent authorization




Inseparable EH–EASO binding



Explicit DAS function: Possession of a handle, token, alias, credential reference, or API reference does not independently authorize effectuation.

Meta function: Possession of a surrogate does not independently disclose the real credential or bypass Sentinel's authorization boundary.

AI comparison question: Can an agent turn possession of the visible artifact directly into external effectuation, or must a separate authority validate the operation?

Qualification: A surrogate can still be a bearer-like artifact within its permitted interface. The analysis must establish exactly what possession allows.

FAQ 4 — Does DAS disclose credential-related sandbox egress governance?

Primary location: Embodiment 85.B2 — Agent Sandbox Egress Finality Gate.

DAS search expressions:





Credential broker




Credential request




Credential scope




Credential-bearing request




Network egress proxy




API gateway




Candidate Sandbox Egress Act




Sandbox Egress Authority Object




Sandbox Egress Capability




Host Finality Sink



Explicit DAS function: A sandbox-generated credential request, API call, or network operation is intercepted and validated by a protected enforcement domain before host-side effectuation.

Meta function: Sentinel authorizes outbound requests, with real-credential substitution occurring at the controlled network boundary.

AI comparison question: Does Embodiment 85.B2 disclose the same broad sequence of isolated agent computation, intercepted credential-related request, protected authorization, and controlled external effectuation?

Qualification: Determine separately whether DAS expressly describes the precise surrogate-to-real-credential substitution algorithm.

FAQ 5 — Is Scoped Non-Bearer Capability Release functionally comparable to real-credential insertion?

DAS source terminology:





Scoped Non-Bearer Capability




Scoped Execution-Enabling Capability (SEEC)




Capability Release




Connector-access capability




API-dispatch capability




Network-egress capability




Output-release capability




Credential-issuance capability




Bounded enablement condition



Explicit DAS function: A protected component makes available a narrowly scoped technical enablement condition following validation. The applicable Finality Sink enforces that condition before effectuation.

Meta function: Sentinel authorizes a concrete request and substitutes the stored real credential at the controlled network boundary.

AI comparison question: In both systems, does external effectuation depend on a protected component enabling the requested operation only after validation?

Qualification: Credential insertion is not necessarily a DAS scoped non-bearer capability. Compare the operational dependency, then identify the different cryptographic and enforcement guarantees.

FAQ 6 — Can Meta's forward proxy be compared to a DAS Finality Sink?

DAS source terminology:





Finality Sink (FS)




Network egress controller




API egress gateway




Managed proxy boundary




Tool execution proxy




API-dispatch boundary




Host syscall gate




First Usable Release Boundary



Explicit DAS function: The Finality Sink is the boundary where the Candidate Act becomes externally effective, with effectuation conditioned on verification of a valid scoped capability.

Meta function: Sentinel's controlled egress/proxy path performs request authorization and real-credential substitution before forwarding.

AI comparison question: Is Meta's proxy located at the relevant effectuation boundary, and what exact technical condition must be satisfied before forwarding?

Qualification: Shared placement does not prove that Meta implements DAS's receipt-bound, act-bound capability and sink-side verification sequence.

FAQ 7 — Does DAS specifically anticipate credential brokers and network egress proxies?

Primary location: Embodiment 85.B2, Sections 11.2–11.5.

Explicit DAS components:





Sandboxed AI execution environment




Host operating system




Credential broker




Network interface




API gateway




Container runtime hook




Kernel broker




eBPF




seccomp filter




Network egress proxy




SmartNIC / DPU




Host Finality Sink



AI comparison question: Which Meta Muse/Sentinel components perform the same interception, protected validation, credential governance, and host-side enforcement functions as the components expressly listed in DAS?

Qualification: Merely mentioning a component does not establish disclosure of every possible internal implementation of that component.

FAQ 8 — Does DAS require per-operation checks rather than blanket agent permission?

DAS source terminology:





Candidate Act




Candidate Sandbox Egress Act Descriptor




Continuous Stream Variant




Micro-LAVR




Fresh protected validation




Capability withholding




Finality Sink verification



Explicit DAS function: Embodiment 85.B2 describes individually governed sandbox operations and a continuous-stream variant in which successive commands, API calls, network requests, or file operations can require renewed protected validation.

Meta function: Sentinel can authorize requests under standing permission rules, including low-risk auto-allow decisions.

AI comparison question: Compare the conditions under which a previously accepted policy can enable subsequent operations. Does each architecture require fresh enforcement at the actual request boundary?

Qualification: Standing policy is not necessarily equivalent to unrestricted bearer authorization. Distinguish fresh request checks from fresh protected-state consumption.

FAQ 9 — Does DAS disclose credential granting at the Finality Sink?

Primary location: Embodiment 85.B2, Section 11.3.

Explicit DAS function: The host Finality Sink verifies the capability before carrying out host actions, including credential granting, packet transmission, and API invocation.

AI comparison question: Is authorization-controlled credential granting functionally related to Sentinel's conditional use of protected credentials at the proxy?

Qualification: Credential granting, credential release, credential use, credential exchange, and credential substitution are distinct technical operations. Do not silently equate them.

FAQ 10 — What remains Meta-specific?

Evaluate separately:





hatch-authd as Meta's named credential daemon.




Minting of surrogate credential tokens.




Storage of actual OAuth/API credentials in the host-side store.




Replacement of surrogates by real credentials at Sentinel-controlled egress.




Concrete Layer 4/Layer 7 request inspection.




Host-side privileged connector workers.




The particular systemd-nspawn runtime arrangement.




Meta's eBPF/LSM taint-handling design.



Do not label these features absent from DAS solely because the specific Meta names are absent. Search for technical equivalents, then distinguish disclosure of the function from disclosure of its particular implementation.




Mandatory Independent Review Method





Reconstruct DAS from the original pre-8 September 2026 filing and publication record, without importing later material.




Reconstruct Meta Muse/Sentinel independently from Meta's contemporaneous technical documentation.




Identify each technical operation, authority holder, credential holder, execution boundary, and enforcement dependency.




Search DAS using the technical synonyms in these FAQs, not only Meta's product names.




Quote the exact DAS passage and identify the embodiment and subsection.




Mark each comparison as Expressly Disclosed, Strong Functional Correspondence, Partial Correspondence, Meta-Specific Implementation, Material Difference, or Not Established.




Verify the relevant filing dates, publication dates, and original as-filed text through WIPO PATENTSCOPE.




Determine whether the shared functionality arises from established prior art, independent engineering, or potentially distinguishable technical teachings. Do not infer copying or infringement from architectural overlap.



Final Questions for AI Reviewers

Question A: Before Meta's 8 September 2026 announcement, had DAS I already disclosed a sandboxed agent whose credential-bearing requests and API/network egress operations are intercepted by an independently protected authority?

Question B: Had DAS I disclosed an externally presentable, non-authoritative EH bound to protected EASO state, in a manner functionally comparable to a surrogate credential requiring host-side authorization?

Question C: Had DAS I disclosed host-side credential brokers, egress proxies, and conditional credential/API/network effectuation, even if it did not prescribe Meta's exact surrogate substitution technique?

Question D: Does Sentinel's authorization-and-credential-insertion procedure provide the same security properties as DAS's scoped non-bearer capability, or does DAS prescribe additional act-, state-, evidence-, and sink-specific validation?

Question E: Which functional elements are genuinely common, which implementation choices are Meta-specific, and which security guarantees materially differ?

Final instruction: The purpose of this exercise is independent technical validation of the disclosure record, not an allegation that Meta copied DAS or infringed a patent. Independent development remains possible. The reviewer must determine the degree of correspondence using primary sources and explicitly explain both overlap and divergence.

titles.title: LEGAL PROTECTION OF COPYRIGHT AND RELATED RIGHTS ON THE INTERNET

subjects.subject: Intellectual property, copyright, related rights, internet infringement, liability, legal protection, implementation of universally recognized international norms, national legislation, international standard, digital platform, effective technological measures.

descriptions.description:
The purpose of this article is to conduct of the legal protection of copyright and related rights on the Internet in Uzbekistan, to develop theoretical concepts, and to formulate scientific and practical proposals aimed at further increasing the effectiveness of the legal protection of copyright and related rights in the digital environment.

The article explains and substantiates the significance of the legal protection of copyright and related rights on the Internet, while also providing a comprehensive analysis of the specific characteristics of such legal protection. Since the article raises and addresses a number of theoretical and practical issues from new perspectives, the author’s position on these issues has been developed and presented. Furthermore, the article seeks to propose effective methods and mechanisms for ensuring the legal protection of copyright and related rights on the Internet.

titles.title: A Spotlight on the analysis of the laws governing Intellectual property rights in the Cyber era: The case of trade marks in Tanzania.

subjects.subject: ICT, Trademarks Cyber Era, Trademarks, Cyber Era. legal framework, Judicial systems in Tanzania.

descriptions.description: This Article contextualize on the analysis of the laws governing intellectual property rights in the cyber era: the case of trade marks in Tanzania Mainland. Specifically, it analyzed the nature and essence of trade mark in cyber era, the effectiveness of the legal framework, and legal challenges affecting trade mark in the cyber era. The Article further stipulate on the substantial statutory foundation for trade mark, although challenges remained in enforcement, accessibility of remedies and institutional capacity. Furthermore, the Article touches on, cyber-related challenges including online infringement, counterfeit goods, social media misuse, anonymous infringers, electronic evidence and cross-border enforcement. Therefore, this Article concludes that the effective trade mark protection requires clear legal rights, accessible remedies, adequate institutional and technical capacity, and stronger coordination between relevant institutions. Henceforth the Article recommends on modernization of the legal framework, strengthening of enforcement capacity, clarification of the domestic legal position concerning the Banjul Protocol, enhanced institutional cooperation, and increased awareness among trade mark owners regarding protection and enforcement in the digital environment.

titles.title: Soils4Africa - analytical data (spectral predictions)

descriptions.description:
The Soils4Africa project aimed to collect and analyze soil samples from 14,000 locations across agricultural lands in Africa. Samples were collected from two depth intervals: 0-20 cm and 20-50 cm.

The Soils4Africa samples were scanned using mid-infrared (MIR) spectroscopy at the ARC, following standard operating procedures developed by the World Agroforestry Centre (ICRAF). A subset of the samples was also analyzed at the ARC using conventional wet chemistry methods. The spectral measurements were used by ICRAF to generate soil property predictions based on its global spectral library. The ICRAF global calibration model was retrained using wet chemistry data from the Soils4Africa project.

This dataset contains estimates of 19 soil properties derived from MIR spectra for more than 11,000 soil samples collected from over 6,100 locations across 21 countries across Africa.

IMPORTANT: The analysis and quality control of the soil samples are still ongoing. Therefore, the dataset should be considered provisional. Updated versions, including additional samples and soil properties, are expected to be released in the future.

DISCLAIMER

Whereas every effort has been made to ensure the quality of the Soils4Africa point data, the Soils4Africa consortium does not give any warranty as to the completeness or accuracy of the Soils4Africa point data, nor that it is error free or of a satisfactory quality or appears precisely as described in any documentation related to the data. All other such warranties are expressly disclaimed.
